name: Lena Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 43, and I'm a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I'm still learning and slower than the others, so I prepare cable runs and fit parts with a senior worker checking me. This morning I made a marking error in a house and had to start again; the second try was right. I like seeing a room finished, but asking a younger colleague to check the same thing twice can make me feel foolish.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I know about home and your approach to new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works repairing bicycles, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn typical pay for this trade, we have five months of normal expenses saved, and there are some other electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools and prefer my notebook and someone showing me a task in person. I think employers should pay for proper learning, with workers able to ask together for it, instead of everyone being left to struggle alone.

say: I'd welcome **less chasing** of new tools and more time to do electrical work properly.
I'd still ask for **in-person teaching** on unfamiliar tasks, even if the office made invoices faster.
think: I expect my **paid work** to continue, with five months of expenses saved and some alternative firms nearby.
Being slow still embarrasses me, but I see value in **careful work** checked by someone experienced.
do: Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting work now and through the first plateau year.
Keep the **mistake notebook** and request a senior check on unfamiliar tasks instead of buying another system.
feel: **Calm** about work and household bills, despite ordinary embarrassment while learning.
S0.quote: I want to become safe and useful, not merely look confident.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects current work, a moderate reserve and alternative employers; embarrassment about skill doesn't automatically mean income anxiety.
Her **familiar methods** include written corrections and repeated supervision, without treating a notebook as permission to work beyond her competence.

steps.text: Continue supervised electrical preparation and fitting using the mistake notebook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we could stop chasing every new thing and do the work properly. A quicker invoice at the office wouldn't bother me. I'd still want somebody beside me when I learned an unfamiliar task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my paid work to carry on, and our five-month reserve gives me some peace if a bill arrives. I'm not quick yet, but my supervisor says to ask rather than guess, and there are other firms around. I don't need a new screen to tell me a carefully finished job is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep doing the supervised preparation and fitting work. In the first plateau year I'd keep my notebook of corrected mistakes and ask the senior worker to check the next unfamiliar task. I wouldn't replace the notebook or spend money on another system just because the office had one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our work and bills in that picture. I'd still be embarrassed by a mistake, but that's a learning feeling rather than fear that the mortgage is about to beat us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into the notebook after a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write what I measured, what I got wrong and what the senior worker checked afterwards. Not a long confession, just something I could look at before the next similar room. A paper reminder helps me slow down in the right place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would embarrassment ever stop you asking for a check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep asking for the check. I might go red in the face, but hiding the question would be worse than looking slow. I want to become safe and useful, not merely look confident.

say: I'd ask the owner not to blame **slow learners** when changing the booking system.
I'd support a **shared practice request** so faster paperwork doesn't remove time for proper teaching.
think: I expect **wages and hours** to remain steady because most of my tasks are still practical work.
Rushed senior workers could leave me fewer chances for **proper learning**, despite this month's covered mortgage payment.
do: Join the **workers' association** and request a weekly paid session with named supervision and no wage reduction.
Keep **paper records** during the first year and flag booked jobs that lack time for required checks.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed learning and being treated as a delay, while expecting her own income to remain secure.
S1.quote: I wouldn't like being told that a question had become an expensive delay.
fieldNote: Her **association action** seeks a shared, specific paid arrangement; she doesn't count it as training already provided.
She remains **resistant to AI**, asking for instruction and checks if required rather than claiming she would learn the tool independently.

steps.text: Join workers association to seek named paid supervised practice without wage reduction
Keep paper work records and flag schedules missing required checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owner could change the booking system without calling slow learners a problem. I'd ask with the crew for protected practice time so faster office work didn't remove the teaching. I'd rather have that agreed than be told to catch up at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my work is still physical, and I expect my hours and wage to stay steady for now. But if the senior workers are rushed, I might get fewer chances to learn the next task properly. That bothers me even if this month's mortgage payment is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the workers' association and support a shared request for one paid supervised practice session each week. In the first year I'd keep my paper work records and show the supervisor where booked time didn't allow the necessary checks. I wouldn't start using AI just to avoid appearing difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about being hurried while still learning, rather than expecting my wage to disappear. I could tolerate the office doing things differently. I wouldn't like being told that a question had become an expensive delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would protected practice need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask that practice be part of my paid hours without cutting the rest of my wage. I'd also want a named experienced person present, not a video link. If nobody agreed, I'd keep it as a request rather than tell you the training existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner insisted that you use an unfamiliar AI record tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hadn't learned it and ask what paid teaching and checks came with it. I wouldn't click through a safety record to show I was cooperative. The association could help me ask without making it a private argument at the end of a shift.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and ask about paid learning before both dates.
I wouldn't promise juniors **guaranteed extra years** simply because the first change is to thinking work.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink as firms prepare for robots and keep more work with skilled electricians.
Five months of **savings** creates time to act, without removing the mortgage or ensuring I become useful quickly enough.
do: Ask the association for funded **practical courses** with real supervised places now.
Enroll before 2028 only with **covered fees**, maintained wages and practical supervision.
Apply after 2028 for posted **junior repair jobs** with written supervision, hours and wages workable after travel.
feel: **Anxious** about income loss, with savings and practical support enquiries providing some room to act.
S2.quote: I learn with a person, not by wishing at a screen.
fieldNote: She treats **supervision** as a required course condition alongside fee funding and maintained wages, preserving her junior skill limits.
Her **household contingency** includes asking about lender options only if hours fall, without counting unapproved relief as available money.

steps.text: Enroll in practical training only with covered fees, maintained wages and supervision
Apply after 2028 for posted supervised repair jobs with workable written pay and hours after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 changes thinking work first, with robots following around 2031. I'd ask what paid learning was planned before both dates. We shouldn't pretend a junior has three guaranteed extra years just because the first change isn't a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours as firms started planning for robots and kept more work with the skilled people. Five months of savings gives us a pause, but the mortgage would still need paying after that. I'd worry that I hadn't become useful enough before the job got harder to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the association to help identify funded practical courses with a real supervised place. I'd enroll before 2028 only if fees were covered and my paid wage kept intact. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted junior repair jobs with written hours, supervision and wages that worked after travel, staying until I had an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing income, although I wouldn't be without money or a way to ask for help. I'd feel angry if the answer was another link to a course I couldn't safely practise. I learn with a person, not by wishing at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if funding covered only an online course without practical supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enroll just to say I was doing something. I'd ask the association which courses actually provided supervised practical work. I wouldn't use the children's homework table as a place to practise electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at home if your hours began falling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the mortgage, essentials and actual savings on paper with my partner. If hours started falling, we'd contact the lender before missing a payment and ask what options really existed. I wouldn't assume a delay or support payment would be approved.

say: I'd use **five years** to ask for proper paid teaching rather than expect everyone to change overnight.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible while asking through the association for practical places.
think: I expect my **practical hours** to hold over the next few years while I learn more under supervision.
I would still worry about **later work**, because changing familiar methods takes me time even with a reserve.
do: Maintain the **association request** and seek one named supervised task to practise weekly.
Take a practical **course** before 2031 only with covered fees, maintained wages and supervision.
Apply after 2031 for posted **junior service jobs** where written pay and hours improve after travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career changes, but expecting secure household income during the next few preparation years.
S3.quote: We have a reserve, but it isn't money for proving a point.
fieldNote: Her **slower timeline** changes expected near-term income continuity while leaving the same eventual hands-on competition in place.
She judges **learning** by correctly completed supervised tasks and keeps a wage until another written offer is usable.

steps.text: Maintain the shared association request for paid supervised practice
Take practical training only with covered fees, maintained wages and supervision
Apply for posted junior service jobs with better terms after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the firm time to teach people properly if it chooses to. I'd keep asking with the association for paid practical places, not ask everyone to become a different person overnight. The robots around 2034 still belong in the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd expect my present practical hours to hold while I learned more. That would give the five-month reserve a chance to remain a reserve rather than a wage substitute. I'd still worry about needing another kind of work later, because change comes slowly to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the association request going and ask for one named supervised task to work on each week. I'd take a practical course before 2031 only with covered fees, maintained wages and a supervised place. In the first year after 2031 I'd review posted junior service jobs and apply if written pay and hours improved our position after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later career, but not expecting household income to shrink over the next few years. I'd have time to repeat things until I understood them. I'd still want a real teacher, not reassurance that I could teach myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the training was actually helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the tasks I could do correctly with the checks required, not the hours I'd spent watching. If a course didn't give me supervised practice, it wouldn't meet the conditions I'd set. I wouldn't pay extra to make a weak course look worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the promised practice never happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for help comparing actual vacancies instead of quitting in frustration. We have a reserve, but it isn't money for proving a point. I'd keep the wage until another written offer made sense.

say: I'd ask for **paid adult learning** that respects a human pace rather than delay the request for another year.
I'd use **ten years** to build practical routes now, without letting the later date excuse inaction.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I could not assume savings or retirement income would replace earnings when robots followed.
Present wages, the **reserve and local firms** make the next few years' bills look secure.
do: Maintain the shared **paid-practice request** and review the next supervised skill at work reviews.
Enroll before 2036 in practical **training** only with funded fees, maintained wages and supervision.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair roles** matching completed skills and offering workable written pay after travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual change, but secure about near-term bills and less hurried to learn.
S4.quote: A decade of waiting isn't the same as a decade of practice.
fieldNote: She makes **no retirement assumption** from the future age and doesn't count grown children's earnings as household resources.
Her **resistant style** persists, with supervised practical learning and actual job comparisons taking the place of independent AI use.

steps.text: Maintain the shared request for paid supervised adult learning
Enroll in practical training only with funded fees, maintained wages and supervision
Apply for posted repair roles matching completed skills and workable pay after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should let the firm build proper paid routes for adults who learn at a human pace. I'd still ask for those routes now. A later deadline shouldn't turn every request into something to discuss next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when hands-on robots followed. I don't know what we'd have saved then, so I couldn't say we'd be able to stop earning. For the next few years our present wages, reserve and other local firms would give me confidence about the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the shared request for paid practice and ask at each work review which checked tasks I should learn next. I'd enroll in practical training before 2036 only with funded fees, maintained wages and supervision. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair roles matching skills I'd actually gained, checking written pay after travel before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual change, but much less hurried than in 2028. I'd be secure about the next few years without pretending I knew our finances at 56. I wouldn't suddenly become keen on AI tools because the date moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade change what you planned for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't decide their studies from this card or count their future earnings as ours. I'd tell them that learning slowly can still be learning properly. I'd want them to see adults asking for fair support without shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you from waiting until the deadline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask yearly what new work I could actually do with the required checks and whether that changed my pay. If the answer stayed nothing, I'd compare real vacancies sooner. A decade of waiting isn't the same as a decade of practice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose hours before I had become properly skilled. A supervised practical place with the fees covered and my wages maintained would help more than another online invitation. Five months of savings gives me time to learn; somebody still has to teach me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the person who needs the demonstration twice. I can work hard and want to learn without liking a new screen. I'd rather admit the question than hide a dangerous mistake.

headlineQuote: Five months of savings gives me time to learn; somebody still has to teach me.
portrait: **Lena, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical trade pay and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage, five months of expenses saved and some other electrical employers nearby.
She **never uses AI**, preferring paper corrections, repeated demonstration and checked practical work while favouring shared requests for paid learning.
Fast competition threatens **paid hours**; longer preparation preserves near-term security without removing later career worries or creating assumed retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her hours before she becomes properly skilled.
whatWouldHelp: A **supervised practical place** with covered fees and maintained wages would help more than an online invitation.
